Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq with Mr. Ahsanul Karim, Mr. Faheemul Huq and Mr. Khairul Alam Chowdhury ------ For the petitioner 
Mr. Amirul Islam with, Ms. Tania Amir and Mr. Anwar Patwary ------ For the opposite party
parties:
Reckitt Benckiser (Bangladesh) Ltd
Vs.
Oram Limited, Sel Centre
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why order No. 3 dated 16.8.2007 passed the District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 661 of 2007 should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. Of the 3(three) arbitrator's Mr. Justice K.M. Hasan gave a dissenting award and thus because of the majority derision the award went in favour of the opposite party. Thereafter the present petitioner filed an application before the District Judge, Dhaka under section 42 read with section 43 of the Arbitration Act 2001 (the Act) with the prayer for setting aside the award. The said application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 661 of 2007. 

 4. From the facts as stated in the revision application it appeared that the learned District Judge by his order dated 25.7.2007 fixed 9.8.2007 for hearing the maintainability of the application and then the hearing was adjourned to 16.8.2007 as the learned District Judge went on leave. On 16.8.2007 the opposite party entered appearance in the said arbitration miscellaneous case and filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) read with section 42 of the Act, with the prayer to return the application filed by the petitioner for setting aside the award given by the majority arbitrators mainly on the ground that the arbitration in which the award was given being an international commercial arbitration, the forum for setting aside the same was this Division. And on the very day. the learned District Judge returned the said application to the present petitioner "for filing the same to the competent court" on the view that the application was not maintainable as the central management of one of the two parties to the arbitration is being exercised from U.K. Being aggrieved by the said order of the learned District Judge the petitioner has obtained the present rule. 

 6. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner with Mr. Ahsanul Karim, Mr. Fahimul Haque and Mr. Khairul Alam Chowdhury in reply to the said submissions of Mr. Amirul Islam submitted that the very order passed by the learned District Judge impugned in the revision application having prima facie shown that he neither set aside the award nor refused to set aside the award under sub-section (1) of section 42 of the Act but returned the application filed by the petitioner to it no appeal would lie before this court as contemplated in section 48 of the Act, so the petitioner had no other alternative but to file the revision application before this court and in the facts and circumstances of the instant case the revision application is very much maintainable. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq further submitted that sections 7 and 53 of the Act have got no manner of application in the instant case as with the award given by the arbitral tribunal the arbitration proceeding ended, therefore, by invoking those sections of the Act the revisional jurisdiction of this court under section 115(1) of the Code cannot be ousted. He further submitted that the order impugned having been passed by the learned District Judge on an application filed by the opposite party under section 151 of the Code the revision application is quite maintainable, consequently this Division has the jurisdiction to see as to whether the learned District Judge committed any error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in passing the same. 

 A mere reading of section 42 (1) of the Act shows that the “আদালত” has been given wide power to set aside an award given by an arbitral tribunal except an international commercial Arbitration (আন্তর্জাতিক বানিজ্যিক সালিশে) if an application is filed by a party to the arbitration proceeding within 60 days of the receipt of the award. Sub section (2) of section 42 of the Act has given this Division power to set aside an award under the same condition in case of an international commercial arbitration. The “আদালত” has been defined in clause (kha) of section 2 of the Act, 

 "In the facts and circumstances of the case and legal position, I am of the opinion chat application is not maintainable in its present form and as such this application is hereby returned to the respondent-petitioner for filing the same to the competent court" 

 10. From the above. it is apparent that the learned District Judge did not say anything about the merit of the award given by the majority arbitrators, but simply returned the application to the petitioner filed under section 42 of the Act as being hot maintainable. So in our opinion, the question of filing of an appeal before this court as provided in section 48 of the Act does not arise at all. And therefore, obviously, except availing the revisional jurisdiction as provided in section 115(1) of the Code the petitioner' had no other forum “আদালত” as stipulated in section 42 of the Act, being the District Judge, any order passed by him not being appealable within the Meaning of section 48 of the Act is very much amendable to the revisional jurisdiction of this Division. In the case of A.K.M. Ruhul Amin Versus District Judge and Appellate Election Tribunal heard analogously along with 3(three) other appeals the Appellate Division held that Court of District Judge is subject to both appellate and revisiond jurisdiction of this Division and in exercising revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code against the decision of any election Appellate Tribunal this Division can grant any relief to which any aggrieved party is entitled to under the Ordinance, It may be stated that the said cases arose under the provision of local government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 against the judgment passed by the District Judge as Election Tribunal which was made final under section 29 thereof. So in the instant case the impugned order passed by the District Judge not being appealable the petitioner rightly invoked the revisional jurisdiction of this Court. We also do not find any rational in the submission of Mr. Amirul Islam that the revision application is not maintainable in law inasmuch as the impugned order was passed by the learned District Judge on the application filed by the opposite party under section 151 of the Code. 

 11. Section 7 of the Act has provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force where any of the parties to the arbitration agreement resorts to a legal proceedings against the other party, no court shall have authority to hear any legal proceedings except in so far as provided by this Act. Section 24 of the Act, has specifically provided that the arbitral tribunal shall not be obliged to follow the provisions of the Code and the Evidence Act. Section 25 of the Act has further provided that the arbitral tribunal in proceeding with the arbitration shall follow the procedure as determined by the parties subject to the provisions of the Act. Section 53 of the Act has also provided that where with respect to an arbitration agreement any application is made in any court under the Act that court alone shall have the jurisdiction over the said arbitration proceeding and all subsequent proceedings arising out of the agreement and the arbitration proceedings can be taken in that court only and in no other court. From the provisions of the Act as discussed above it is clear that the provisions of the other laws particularly the Code and the Evidence Act have not been made applicable in case of an arbitration proceeding arising out of an arbitration agreement and the Act has been given the overriding power over all the laws in Bangladesh. But in the instant ease the arbitration proceeding having ended with the giving of the award by the arbitral tribunal those provisions of the Act cannot be pleaded as a bar in ousting the revisional jurisdiction of this court to see the propriety of an order passed by the District Judge as has happened in the instant case as discussed hereinbefore, so we hold that the instant revision application filed under section 115(1) of the Code against the impugned order is very much maintainable and this court can very much see whether the learned District Judge committed any error of law resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice in passing the same and accordingly, we propose to dispose of this revision application on merit. 

 12. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, by referring to articles 131,133,135 and 136 of the Articles of Association of the petitioner company submitted that if those articles are read together along with the definition of the Bangladeshi Company as given in arouse clauses of section 2 of the Companies Act, 1994 (the Act, 1994) it would appear that it is the Board of Directors of the company which controls the affairs and the business of the company. Mr. Huq by referring to article 131 made further specific submission that the said article having specifically provided that all Board meetings of the company shall be held in Bangladesh and the Directors shall be entitled to exercise their powers as Directors only when and whist they are respectively in Bangladesh primafacie shows that central management and control of the company is done in Bangladesh. Mr. Huq also submitted that in view of the provisions of article 131 it cannot be said that the petitioner company is a subsidiary company of Reckitt Benckiser PLC U.K. and therefore, the arbitration in question was not an international commercial arbitration and as such the District Judge had the jurisdiction to dispose of the application filed before him under section 42 of the Act on merit. Mr. Huq further submitted that Government of Bangladesh has but its share in the petitioner company and two of its Directors one of the rank of additional secretary and another of the rank of joint secretary of the Ministry of Industries are nominated by the Government, so the employees of the company are public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Penal Code and moreso the petitioner company being a listed Company its regulating authority is the Security and Exchange Commission of the government of Bangladesh how can it be said that the central management and control of the company is in U.K. as found by the learned District Judge. Mr. Huq lastly submitted that the quantum of the share of the share-holding of a company is not the deciding factor for the management and control of the company and the share-holder cannot have any role to play in the affairs and management of a company and it is the Board of Directors which definitely control and manage the affairs of the company; further majority Directors of the Board of Directors being Bangladeshi and the company being registered in Bangladesh having its registered office here the learned District Judge was absolutely wrong in holding that the central control and management of the petitioner company being in U.K. the arbitration in which the award was given was an international commercial arbitration. Mr. Haque further pointed out that article 136 having clearly provided that the chief executive officer of the company being the Managing Director shall be appointed by the Board of Directors including the power to remove or dismiss him, by no stretch of imagination it can be said that the control and central management of the petitioner company is in U.K. and not in Bangladesh. Mr. Haque in support of his contention has referred to the case of Punjab Ali Pranianik and others Versus Mohd. Mokarram Hossain reported in 29 DLR (SC) 185. 

 16. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case sub clause (B) of clause (M) of section 2 is relevant. A reading of sub clause (B) along with clause (gal primafacie shows that to make an arbitration. "international commercial arbitration” it must be an arbitration relating to a dispute arising out of legal relationships, whether contractual or not considered as commercial under the law in force in Bangladesh and where at least one of the parties is a company or an association or a body of individuals whose central management and control is exercised in any country other than Bangladesh. So let us now see whether the central management and control of the petitioner namely, Reckitt, Benckiser (Bangladesh) Ltd. is exercised in any country other than Bangladesh, that is, in U.K. 

 18. Mr. Amirul Islam gave much emphasis on the fact that Reckitt Bencksier PLC U.K. being the majority share-holders of the petitioner company it became a foreign-entity, so the control and management of the petitioner company is exercised from U.K. The argument of Mr. Amirul Islam is absolutely misconceived. The reason being that the share-holders of a company never manage the affairs and business of a company and it is the Board of Directors created for the said purpose which control and manage the affairs of the company. We also like to observe that the directors of a company are not the agents or representatives of the share-holders of the company. A person both natural and juridical may hold share of a company but because of such holding of shares in the company he or it cannot have a say in the management or control of the affairs and business of the company. There is also no bar in law in holding share of a company by a foreign entity as in the instant case but that does not mean that if a foreign entity holds majority shares of a Bangladeshi company the central management and control of a Bangladeshi company shall automatically by exercised by the foreign entity, here Reckitt Benckiser PLC U.K. We get support of our view from the case of Punjab Ali Pramanik and others versus Mohd Mokarram Hossein reported in 29 DLR (SC) 185 as referred to by Mr. Haque. 

 21. We also do not find any factual and legal basis of the submission of Mr. Amirul Islam that the petitioner company is the subsidiary company of Reckit Benckiser PLC , U.K. To make a company subsidiary of another certain conditions as laid down in sub sections (2) (3) and (4) of section 2 of the Act, 1994 must be fulfilled. But those are totally absent in the instant case. A reading of articles 133 and 134 of the Articles of Association wherein the powers of the Directors have been articulated it appeared to us that the Board of Directors of the petitioner company is quite independent and in no way subservient and controlled by the Board of Directors of Reckitt Bencksier PLC. U.K. The thing will be more clear if we refer to the interpretation clause of the petitioner company which has specifically said to the effect "The company" means RECKITT BENCKISER (BANGLADESH) LIMITED. In the revision application it has been categorically stated that the petitioner is a listed company with Dhaka Stock Exchange and Chittagong Stock Exchange. The regulatory and controlling authority of the petitioner is the security and Exchange Commission (SEC), a statutory authority of Bangladesh. In the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner it has further been stated that all the meetings of the Board of Directors of the company are held in Bangladesh and never in the history of the company any Board Meeting of the company ever held outside Bangladesh. Although the opposite party made statements in the affidavit filed before this Court as well as before the District Judge that the petitioner company is a subsidiary company of the U.K. entity rather than a fully independent company and that every step taken by the petitioner is determined by the Reckitt Benckiser PLC U.K. no paper/document has been filed to substantiate the said statements and to show further that any Board Meeting of the petitioner company ever held outside Bangladesh. We have also perused the lower court's record from where it is clear that not a single scrap of paper was filed to show that the central control and management of the petitioner company is used to be exercised by Reckitt Benckiser PLC U.K. It is an admitted fact that the petitioner company is incorporated in Bangladesh having its registered office here and the "Memorandum and Articles of Association of the Company" prima facie manifest that it is a Bangladeshi company. We are of the further view that mere similarity of the nature of the business of a company shall not make it subsidiary of another unless the conditions as stipulated in sub sections (2) (3) and (4) of section 2 of the Act 1994 are present. We are constrained to hold that the finding of the learned District Judge to the effect that the central management and control of Reckitt Benckiser (Bangladesh) Ltd. is exercised by Reckitt Bencksier PLC. U.K. has got no factual and legal basis. Incoming to the said finding the learned District Judge has not at all considered the various articles of the Articles of Association of the petitioner company as well as its Memorandum.
